One of Josie McDermott’s best compositions

I believe that Altan’s version is the most listened to as they just called it “McDermott’s” which explains why it was submitted in 2005 under this name. Of course it does appear on The Session as “Father O’Grady’s Trip To Bocca” and it is composed by flute player, Josie McDermott. But there are many tunes with the name McDermott’s. Many times it is a different McDermott. The only shortcoming of this site is that once a tune, jig or reel is filed under one name (like McDermott’s) there is not room for another tune with the same name unless it is renamed. Or as in this case of the same tune appearing more than once under a different name.

↳ Posted by jamadairg on September 4th, 2011.

Josie’s sleeve notes =

“… named after a missionary priest from the townland of Bocca, near Ballydreen, Co. Roscommon. On a visit home, he gave Josie a flute and in return asked that ”You’ll make a tune for me“. This is the tune.”

↳ Posted by Kenny on February 2nd, 2012.

Father O’Grady’s Visit To Bocca is actually Bockagh

https://maps.google.com/maps?f=q&source=s_q&hl=en&geocode=&q=Bockagh,+Ireland&aq=0&oq=bockagh&sll=42.746632,-75.770041&sspn=6.445331,9.876709&vpsrc=0&ie=UTF8&hq=&hnear=Bockagh,+County+Roscommon,+Ireland&t=m&z=15&iwloc=A

The above link is from Google Maps and will show you the town-land that Father Peter O’Grady was born. He was born May 23 of 1907 to Peter Grady and Catherine Morrisroe, both from Bockagh, Ballaghadereen, Mayo which today is Roscommon. Ballaghadereen was in Mayo prior to the Irish Revolution and was then re-assigned/evaluated to be part of Roscommon.

Father Peter O’Grady was my granduncle.

↳ Posted by Tommy O'Grady on January 5th, 2013.

Mcdermott’s

This is not the tune McDermott’s on the CD “Round the House and Mind the Dresser”

↳ Posted by ph on June 20th, 2013.

McDermotts

No It is not the same McDermott. The name is not uncommon in both the South and the North of Ireland. McDermott’s is almost like having a tune called O’Brien’s name-wise that is. So there will be other McDermott tunes that do not come from Josie, like Master McDermott’s from a fiddle teacher who came from County Tyrone.

Father O’Grady’s Visit To Bocca, X:4

This is a difficult tune on flute with phrases like “Adde” and “~G3 A GE ~E2 | edcA…” and so on.
It suits the North Connacht style of cuts and throat cuts, ( see Seamus Tierny video above ), so for legato flute players here it is ( Setting #4 ) as played something in the style of June McCormack.
Majestic tune though.

Peace Out
Pat

↳ Posted by Pat Higgins on April 27th, 2022.

Father O’Grady’s Visit To Bocca, X:6

Setting for mouth whistling.

In the high octave of C Major. Wonderful chords published in the last setting, I have used them for this setting. There are some changes in the melody line, this is the setting I’m more used to play.

↳ Posted by Fernando Durbán Galnares on October 12th, 2022.

Father O’Grady’s Visit To Bocca, X:7

This setting is taken from the playing of a duet by two great fluters: Deirdre Havlin (Dee Tasker) and Marcas Ó Murchú.
See this video on Youtube, they play Father O’Grady’s Trip To Bocca / Darby’s Farewell To London …. no indication as to when and where it was recorded, but it’s a great setting and performance, as you’d expect. Apologies for any oversimplifications here of what they play.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7aOWLklQTVE

↳ Posted by Rover on August 23rd, 2023.

Re: Father O’Grady’s Visit To Bocca

Tuuuuuuuuuuuunes!!!, Father O’Grady’s is one of my favourite tunes. Yes your roll notation is fine.

But I think you have a typo in the first half, 5th measure: |fded CAAG| The uppercase C should be lowercase c so it’s in the same octave as the neighboring notes. You can fix this—click on the ABC tab, and then on the “Edit” button, and replace C with c, and it’ll be good to go. (This works only on tunes you’ve submitted. You can’t edit other people’s transcriptions.)

↳ Posted by gimpy on March 30th, 2024.

Father O’Grady’s Visit To Bocca, X:10

This is as close as I could get to Josie’s version from his recording (Darby’s Farewell).

Josie McDermott was born in 1925. Let’s honour his centenary by learning his tunes correctly (i.e. as he composed them and as HE played them)!

EDIT: the last beat of the A part should be a minim, not a crotchet - apologies.
The Session won’t let you edit tunes after you upload them, unfortunately.
